extracted.intended_audience: Cambridge (CIE) IGCSE English Language students preparing Assignment 3 (narrative coursework)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing the Cambridge (CIE) IGCSE Assignment 3 narrative coursework: a 500–800 word fiction piece assessed for content/structure and style/accuracy. Advice covers planning, plot structure, characterisation, setting, language techniques and exam‑specific constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and structure (10 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: 10 marks available for content and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors look for well-defined and developed ideas and images, a convincing overall picture and coherence of plot and structure. Structure into clear paragraphs and a controlled plot is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and accuracy (15 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: 15 marks available for style and accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marks awarded for precise vocabulary, varied sentence structures used for effect, appropriate language and tone for the context, and spelling, punctuation and grammar that are almost always accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word‑count requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Your piece of writing should be between 500 and 800 words in length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only responses within this range are appropriate for the assignment; the task examines writing skill within this constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of fiction must be evident
rubrics_metrics.description: To reach highest marks you must create a developed, well-defined plot and include features of fiction writing, such as characterisation and setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives may be an opening/closing chapter or a short story, but should show fiction techniques rather than simply listing events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single plot focus and limited main characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The best short stories are based on a single plot idea and have a maximum of two main characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep plot simple enough to be coherent and cohesive; too many characters or subplots weakens development in a short piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start at the main setting (exposition guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stick to one main setting and start at the location: do not include a lengthy 'journey' before the main action of your story starts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hook your reader, give clues about later events without revealing everything; build a clear setting paragraph before introducing unnecessary information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan an ending with a resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan your ending with a resolution (decide whether your story will end happily or not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A planned ending avoids abrupt or missing conclusions. You may opt to resolve or end on a deliberate cliff‑hanger (not a sudden/weak ending).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan one main event
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan your writing in an order which takes your character (and reader) on a clear journey by planning one main event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focusing on one central event helps maintain control and coherence within time/word limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a 5-part narrative structure (Freytag's Pyramid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider a five-part narrative structure: Exposition, Rising action, Climax, Falling action, Resolution/Denouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each stage has specific aims: exposition sets scene/hook; rising action builds tension; climax is turning point; falling action shows consequences; resolution ties up or leaves suspense intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: In exposition: hook the reader, decide perspective and tense, introduce up to two characters, use senses to create atmosphere and possibly end with an inciting incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First person 'I' and past tense are easier to control. Employ the five senses and ensure the scene's mood reflects the character's mood (pathetic fallacy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rising action specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Rising action should build tension, drama or interest and directly lead to the climax; it should also develop characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialogue, monologue, and direct or indirect characterisation to create three‑dimensional characters; make events escalate logically to the turning point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax is the turning point where everything changes; the protagonist faces an external problem or internal dilemma and a choice is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence structure, length and language here for dramatic effect to highlight the moment of change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falling action specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Falling action shows consequences of the climax and focuses on characters' thoughts and feelings as a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to further develop characterisation and show aftermath logically linked to the climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution/denouement guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: You can resolve your story, or end on a cliff‑hanger; avoid clichés such as 'I woke up and it was all a dream'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cliff‑hanger should be suspenseful, not abrupt or unearned; consider reflecting back to opening imagery for cyclical structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphing: five or six paragraphs recommended
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative responses should be structured into five or six paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary paragraph lengths for effect; each paragraph should develop separate ideas; poor planning often leads to abrupt or missing endings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tense and perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide which narrative perspective and tense you are going to write in; first person 'I' and the past tense are easier to control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistency; tense/perspective choices affect voice and what information can be shown or told.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural techniques: flashback
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider employing structural techniques, such as a flashback, to give background information and provide context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you use a flashback, ensure you signal it and use past‑tense verbs appropriately; don't confuse chronology unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Build detailed characterisation; characters should represent ideas (hope, strength, abandonment) and undergo development/change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer indirect characterisation ('show') over direct ('tell') to create well‑rounded, engaging characters; limit yourself to two characters in a short piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct vs indirect characterisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct characterisation = writer describes the character (telling). Indirect characterisation = hint via speech, thoughts, interactions (showing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indirect characterisation for more complex, relatable characters; overuse of direct description leads to superficial characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance — use only if relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Your character’s appearance may not always be relevant; include it if it signals something important (e.g., king, soldier, someone in trouble).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facial expressions and short descriptive details are often more effective than long appearance lists; in first person it's rare to describe one's own looks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movements and body language
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe characters through movements and body language to convey emotion and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small actions (head dropping, shuffled steps) reveal character without explicit explanation; verbs are key to showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: If using dialogue, limit it and punctuate speech marks correctly; dialogue should progress characterisation or plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dialogue that doesn't advance the story; choose verbs other than 'said' (whispered, shrieked) to reveal tone, but use sparingly and accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monologue and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Monologue in first person helps readers engage and creates a personal tone; you can create a voice using punctuation and short sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use emotive language and sentence rhythm to reflect character's mental state; short sentences can indicate nervousness or tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Build an effective setting that contributes to atmosphere and mood; the setting should reflect the main character’s mood (pathetic fallacy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensory language (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste); allow a paragraph to set scene; contrast scenes to show change; ensure descriptions build a consistent mood and avoid contradictory images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the reader curious — don't reveal everything
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep your reader guessing and asking questions; do not give too much away all at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use selective detail and gradual revelation (like Taboo game): evoke rather than name everything directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use literary/linguistic devices deliberately
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ devices such as repetition, alliteration, metaphor, personification, onomatopoeia, simile (sparingly), imagery, juxtaposition, emotive language and power verbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition as a motif; avoid comic-book onomatopoeia or ALL CAPS; metaphors can be extended; similes should be used sparingly for impact; ensure devices serve atmosphere/character rather than decorate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word choice: connotations and precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider connotations of words and phrases; choose precise, well‑chosen vocabulary to evoke emotions and reveal character/background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words should contribute to overall atmosphere and effect; avoid over-complicating language—simple words used effectively often have more impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés and overused narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid clichés or over‑used narratives (for example, abandoned cabins in the woods) and tired endings ('it was all a dream').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for originality in situation, detail or voice; clichés lessen engagement and exam marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control use of dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not over‑use dialogue; only use it if it drives forward the plot and you can punctuate it correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inexperienced writers should limit dialogue to essential exchanges that reveal character or move the story on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat ideas for emphasis (motif)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is effective to repeat images or ideas (for example, colours) to create motifs throughout the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition strengthens themes when used purposefully (e.g., repeating 'black and grey' to set mood); avoid meaningless repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence and paragraph lengths for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary sentence structure and length, and paragraph lengths, to keep style and tone dynamic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short sentences can heighten tension; longer sentences can slow pace or describe; use variation deliberately to match narrative moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include characters' thoughts and feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Include your characters’ thoughts and feelings, not just what happens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal reflection deepens characterisation and engages the reader; balance action with internal response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure every chosen word contributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that all the words you choose contribute to the overall atmosphere and effect you want to create.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove irrelevant detail; economy of language in a short piece increases impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical exam tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan carefully (you have limited time); a well organised and thoughtful interpretation of the title is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend about 15 minutes planning; avoid unplanned writing which often leads to weak endings; choose a perspective and stick to it; relate characters to a clear message if appropriate.
